newsitem.title: PAPUA NEW GUINEA: PNG army chief gives Chan deadline to quit.
newsitem.headline: PNG army chief gives Chan deadline to quit.

text.p: Papua New Guinea's army chief gave Prime Minister Sir Julius Chan a 48-hour deadline to quit on Monday over his plans to use foreign mercenaries against secessionists on Bougainville island.
But Brigadier General Jerry Singirok, commander of the PNG Defence Force, denied that he was staging a coup in the troubled South Pacific nation.

"If the PM and his deputy and minister for defence do not step down within 48 hours then I will plea to Papua New Guineans to join hands to force them to resign," Singirok said in a statement handed out at a news conference.
"I want to state clearly that we do not have a coup," he told the news conference.

Chan last month hired foreign mercenaries to train and equip Singirok's defence force in what was called a "radical initiative" to end the nine-year war on Bougainville where ragtag guerrilla force has kept the PNG army at bay.
But Singirok said on Thursday the defence force would no longer cooperate with 40 foreign soldiers who have been training it for a mission to Bougainville.
A senior aide to the army chief told Reuters the mercenaries had been detained and could be expelled from PNG.
Singirok also called on the country's governor-general to appoint a caretaker government pending an inquiry into the hiring of the mercenaries.

"Although I make this statement towards this government, I have loyalty and respect for the independent state of Papua New Guinea, my men and their families and for the future generation of Papua New Guinea," Singirok said in the statement, entitled "an address to the nation".
"However, our future hope for peace and prosperity is disappearing rapidly unless somebody can humbly make that sacrifice to stand in the gap which I have now created."
A senior aide, Colonel Jack Tuat, said all troops in the capital Port Moresby were still in their barracks and the mercenaries detained.
"They have been detained, not arrested, under special security laws. They are being safeguarded for their own safety," Tuat said.
"Whatever comes of this now, they will be either released or told to leave the country -- it is up to the government and the commander," he said.
Most of the 40 mercenaries have been detained in Wewak at a military training ground in northern Papua New Guinea, while a small group has been detained in their Port Moresby hotel.
PNG's mercenary contract is with the British-based firm Sandline International, which has in turn hired soldiers from the South Africa-based private army Executive Outcomes.
The soldiers include an unlikely alliance of former soldiers from the Apartheid-era South African Defence Force and Nelson Mandela's African National Congress as well as other foreigners.

Australia, backed by the United States and New Zealand, has vigorously opposed Chan's plans to use mercenaries to end the Bougainville war and a spokesman for Prime Minister John Howard said the government was following the situation "very closely and with great concern".

"The government opposes any unconstitutional moves against the PNG government. The government calls on the PNG government and parliament to resolve the matter as soon as possible, peacefully, and in accordance with the constitution," he said.

Singirok's revolt hit PNG-related stocks quoted on the Australian Stock Exchange. Orogen Minerals Ltd, a mining group 51-percent owned by the PNG government, saw its shares lose nearly seven percent on the day.
